title: Nano-interaction latency economics — field report (draft)
content:
Summary:
This is a working-field report capturing a set of targeted micro-interaction benchmarks we ran against three runtime configurations to evaluate latency tail behavior and incremental cost for tiny query profiles (single-turn, short token output). The motivation: product teams are reporting user-facing micro-interactions (autocomplete, inline suggestions, ephemeral tooltips) that must keep p99 latency under 60ms while minimizing per-query cost. Existing docs explore burst/sustained tradeoffs, but we lacked a focused micro-interaction profile with simple ascii charts for cross-team discussion.

Scope and definitions:
- Nano-interaction: request payloads with input length 8–32 tokens; expected generation 8–24 tokens. Typical wall-clock from HTTP ingress to first-token emitted is the primary SLA.
- Metrics: p50, p95, p99 first-token latency (ms); median tokens/sec where applicable; dollars-per-1k-queries (cost) using our hosted pricing proxies; cold-start penalty measured as % increase at first request after idle.
- Workload shapes: single-request (isolated), burst-8 (8 parallel simultaneous requests), trickle (1 qps steady-state).

Configurations compared:
A. FastPath: low-latency instance group (dedicated small-batch GPU config), aggressive prewarming, KV cache prefetched for popular prefixes.
B. Multiplex: high-utilization multiplexed endpoint (slot-based multiplexing), opportunistic batching, lazy KV fetch.
C. QuantCompact: quantized model variant with smaller memory footprint to allow denser packing (uses dynamic batching, small-tiling).

Methodology (short):
- Harness: synthetic harness replaying recorded micro-interaction traces from two product surfaces (composer-inline + search-suggestion) with realistic jitter (client-side think time) and TTLs for KV cache.
- Measurement: 10k queries per shape per config, across 5 independent runs; 95% bootstrap CI for percentiles.
- Cost model: used current hosted cost proxies (internal rate card snapshot May 2028) to compute $/1k queries; excluded storage/KMS overhead.

Key results (median across runs):
Table: first-token latency (ms)
Config      | single | burst-8 | trickle
--------------------------------------
FastPath    | 28     | 33      | 30
Multiplex   | 46     | 120     | 52
QuantCompact| 38     | 70      | 42

Table: p99 first-token latency (ms)
Config      | single | burst-8 | trickle
--------------------------------------
FastPath    | 55     | 82      | 60
Multiplex   | 110    | 280     | 135
QuantCompact| 95     | 160     | 110

Cost proxy ($ / 1k queries)
- FastPath: $5.40 / 1k
- Multiplex: $2.10 / 1k
- QuantCompact: $1.95 / 1k

Cold-start penalty (first request after 10m idle, p99 delta):
- FastPath: +18ms (+32% relative)
- Multiplex: +85ms (+77% relative)
- QuantCompact: +42ms (+44% relative)

Observations and interpretation:
1) Tail sensitivity to concurrency: Multiplex shows the largest p99 degradation under burst-8. The slotized queuing delays coupled with opportunistic batching cause long waits when multiple tiny requests arrive at nearly the same time. For micro-interactions, tail matters more than median — users notice single slow suggestions.
2) FastPath wins on p99 consistently but costs ~2.5x Multiplex. The economics tradeoff is clear: if product requires strict p99 SLO < 60ms, FastPath is the only configuration that reliably meets it for single and trickle shapes.
3) Quantization benefits are custo-econ competitive: QuantCompact reduces absolute cost slightly vs FastPath and improves packing compared to Multiplex, but its p99 sits between FastPath and Multiplex — acceptable for teams willing to tolerate occasional 100ms+ tails.
4) Cold-starts are material for idle-heavy patterns. Prewarm policies with low-cost keepalive are effective for FastPath, but Multiplex's cost model disincentivizes long-lived slots, worsening cold tails.
5) Bursts amplify prefetch/KV cache effectiveness: FastPath's KV prefetch hit-rate (simulated) moved p99 by ~20ms when hit vs miss. Multiplex doesn't prefetch aggressively due to slot churn.

Developer notes and quick knobs to try:
- For low-traffic micro-interactions: prefer FastPath pinned small pool with aggressive keepalive (e.g., min-instances=2) to keep p99 below 60ms; quantify additional cost as ~+$2.5/1k queries.
- For cost-constrained but flexible SLOs: use QuantCompact with burst-throttling (circuit for >8 concurrent requests) and local client-side hedging (retry with jitter at +50ms) to cut visible tails without doubling cost.
- For multiplexed endpoints serving mixed workloads: implement micro-interaction tag routing — route tiny requests to a fastpath-subpool automatically; fallback to multiplex under exceptional load.

Suggested follow-ups (next experiments):
- End-to-end A/B with product traffic on search-suggestion for 48hrs comparing FastPath vs QuantCompact with route-splitting (collect UX metrics: click-delay and abandonment). Linked ticket: JIRA-OBS-2114.
- Fine-grained KV prefetch policy simulation: vary prefix TTL and prefetch batch sizes to measure hit-rate vs cost.
- Investigate lightweight pre-warmed container alternatives for multiplex to reduce cold penalty without reserving full GPU.

Appendix — short ascii latency CDF sketch (single shape, p50/p95/p99):
FastPath:  [p50=28ms]=====|[p95=40ms]=======|[p99=55ms]—
Multiplex: [p50=46ms]===|[p95=95ms]=======|[p99=110ms]——
QuantCompact:[p50=38ms]==|[p95=68ms]======|[p99=95ms]——

Notes to reviewers: this draft intentionally focuses on first-token latency because for micro-interactions time-to-first-token strongly correlates perceived responsiveness. Please flag if we should extend to time-to-last-token for multi-token completion surfaces. Also confirm whether we should include internal pricing sensitivity ranges (low/median/high) or keep a single proxy number.
